items.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: And then I’ll listen to Rufus Reid, Ron Carter, Buster Williams and Cecil McBee, George Mraz, you know John Patitucci

ctx.x: Relevant is closer. To be not just relevant but in order for it to be real for each one of these musicians, they really have to — see when I was coming up, and most generations before me, one of the main things we used to listen are the older guys. One of the things they used to tell us is look kid, if you don’t do anything with your music or your instrument, get your own sound. Get your own ability to have a signature sound. Harry Carney — his own sound. Johnny Hodges — his own sound. Duke Ellington — his own…

And he learned how to actually develop, get a voice, and put it out there. And that kind of voice is, it’s possible for anybody to have that voice. Anyone who is passionate about the music, whether they become a professional musician or not, and that really is instructive as to how I think the next level of jazz education needs to be — shall we say — augmented. We just need to find a way to bring personal voice up to the same level as all the other values that we’re trying to instill in the students. Because in…
